claim: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a zoonotic virus from camels causing significant mortality and morbidity in humans in the Arabian Peninsula.
source: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a zoonotic virus from camels causing significant mortality and morbidity in humans in the Arabian Peninsula.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript regarding MERS-CoV epidemiology and camel reservoir.

claim: Long-term MERS-CoV evolution occurs exclusively in camels.
source: We employ structured coalescent models to show that long-term MERS-CoV evolution occurs exclusively in camels, whereas humans act as a transient, and ultimately terminal host.
evidence: This claim is supported by structured coalescent analyses presented in Figure 1 and related text showing camel-centered phylogenetic patterns.

claim: Humans act as a transient and terminal host for MERS-CoV.
source: We employ structured coalescent models to show that long-term MERS-CoV evolution occurs exclusively in camels, whereas humans act as a transient, and ultimately terminal host.
evidence: This is demonstrated through phylogenetic analysis showing human clusters as evolutionary dead-ends nested within camel diversity.

claim: Human outbreaks in the Arabian peninsula are driven by seasonally varying zoonotic transfer of viruses from camels.
source: By analysing the distribution of human outbreak cluster sizes and zoonotic introduction times, we show that human outbreaks in the Arabian peninsula are driven by seasonally varying zoonotic transfer of viruses from camels.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of introduction times shown in Figure 2 identifying seasonal patterns.

claim: Without heretofore unseen evolution of host tropism, MERS-CoV is unlikely to become endemic in humans.
source: Without heretofore unseen evolution of host tropism, MERS-CoV is unlikely to become endemic in humans.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the finding that R0 is below 1.0 and humans represent terminal hosts.

claim: MERS-CoV was first discovered in 2012.
source: The virus, first discovered in 2012 (Zaki et al., 2012; van Boheemen et al., 2012), has caused more than 2000 infections and over 700 deaths, according to the World Health Organization (WHO) (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: MERS-CoV has caused more than 2000 infections and over 700 deaths according to WHO.
source: The virus, first discovered in 2012 (Zaki et al., 2012; van Boheemen et al., 2012), has caused more than 2000 infections and over 700 deaths, according to the World Health Organization (WHO) (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from WHO data.

claim: MERS-CoV infections are observed among the most severely affected individuals, such as older males with comorbidities.
source: Its epidemiology remains obscure, largely because infections are observed among the most severely affected individuals, such as older males with comorbidities (Assiri et al., 2013a; WHO MERS-Cov Research Group, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Some MERS-CoV patients do not recall contact with any livestock, suggesting an unobserved community contribution to the outbreak.
source: While contact with camels is often reported, other patients do not recall contact with any livestock, suggesting an unobserved community contribution to the outbreak (WHO MERS-Cov Research Group, 2013).
evidence: This is based on epidemiological observations cited from WHO research group.

claim: High seroprevalence of MERS-CoV has been shown in camels.
source: Such data have shown high seroprevalence in camels (Müller et al., 2014; Corman et al., 2014; Chu et al., 2014; Reusken et al., 2013; Reusken et al., 2014) and evidence of contact with MERS-CoV in workers with occupational exposure to camels (Reusken et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple serological studies cited.

claim: Workers with occupational exposure to camels show evidence of contact with MERS-CoV.
source: Such data have shown high seroprevalence in camels (Müller et al., 2014; Corman et al., 2014; Chu et al., 2014; Reusken et al., 2013; Reusken et al., 2014) and evidence of contact with MERS-CoV in workers with occupational exposure to camels (Reusken et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by serological studies cited.

claim: A median of 56 separate camel-to-human cross-species transmissions were estimated across 174 MERS-CoV genomes collected from humans.
source: Across 174 MERS-CoV genomes collected from humans, we estimate a median of 56 separate camel-to-human cross-species transmissions (95% highest posterior density (HPD): 48–63).
evidence: This is derived from structured coalescent analysis of sequence data.

claim: A median of 3 human-to-camel migrations were estimated, with 95% HPD interval including zero.
source: While we estimate a median of 3 (95% HPD: 0–12) human-to-camel migrations, the 95% HPD interval includes zero and we find that no such migrations are found in the maximum clade credibility tree (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on structured coalescent analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Substantially higher camel-to-human migration rate estimates were observed than human-to-camel migration rate estimates.
source: Correspondingly, we observe substantially higher camel-to-human migration rate estimates than human-to-camel migration rate estimates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 displaying migration rate estimates.

claim: The vast majority of MERS-CoV evolution is inferred to occur in camels with human outbreaks representing evolutionary dead-ends for the virus.
source: Maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree showing inferred ancestral hosts for MERS-CoV recovered with the structured coalescent. The vast majority of MERS-CoV evolution is inferred to occur in camels (orange) with human outbreaks (blue) representing evolutionary dead-ends for the virus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 phylogenetic tree with host state reconstruction.

claim: Four months (April, May, June, July) show increased odds of MERS-CoV introductions.
source: We identify four months (April, May, June, July) when the odds of MERS-CoV introductions are increased (Figure 2) and four when the odds are decreased (August, September, November, December).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of introduction times shown in Figure 2.

claim: Four months (August, September, November, December) show decreased odds of MERS-CoV introductions.
source: We identify four months (April, May, June, July) when the odds of MERS-CoV introductions are increased (Figure 2) and four when the odds are decreased (August, September, November, December).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of introduction times shown in Figure 2.

claim: Camel calving is reported to occur from October to February.
source: Camel calving is reported to occur from October to February (Almutairi et al., 2010), with rapidly declining maternal antibody levels in calves within the first weeks after birth (Wernery, 2001).
evidence: This is cited from published literature on camel reproduction.

claim: Maternal antibody levels in camel calves decline rapidly within the first weeks after birth.
source: Camel calving is reported to occur from October to February (Almutairi et al., 2010), with rapidly declining maternal antibody levels in calves within the first weeks after birth (Wernery, 2001).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: MERS-CoV may sweep through each new camel generation once critical mass of susceptibles is reached.
source: It is possible that MERS-CoV sweeps through each new camel generation once critical mass of susceptibles is reached (Martinez-Bakker et al., 2014), leading to a sharp rise in prevalence of the virus in camels and resulting in increased force of infection into the human population.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on epidemiological theory cited and observed seasonality patterns.

claim: Little correlation exists between date and size of MERS-CoV introduction (Spearman ρ=0.06, p=0.68).
source: We find little correlation between date and size of introduction (Spearman ρ=0.06, p=0.68).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of introduction dates and cluster sizes.

claim: No trend in human sequence cluster sizes over time was observed.
source: Similarly, we do not observe any trend in human sequence cluster sizes over time (Figure 2B, Spearman ρ=0.06, p=0.68), suggesting that MERS-CoV outbreaks in humans are neither growing nor shrinking in size.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MERS-CoV outbreaks in humans are neither growing nor shrinking in size.
source: Similarly, we do not observe any trend in human sequence cluster sizes over time (Figure 2B, Spearman ρ=0.06, p=0.68), suggesting that MERS-CoV outbreaks in humans are neither growing nor shrinking in size.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of temporal trend in cluster sizes.

claim: Mean R0 value observed in matching simulations is 0.72 (95% percentiles 0.57–0.90).
source: Mean R0 value observed in matching simulations is 0.72 (95% percentiles 0.57–0.90), suggesting the inability of the virus to sustain transmission in humans.
evidence: This is derived from Monte Carlo simulations matching empirical sequence cluster patterns.

claim: R0 for MERS-CoV in humans is likely to be below 1.0.
source: Monte Carlo simulations indicate R0 for MERS-CoV in humans is likely to be below 1.0, with numbers of zoonotic transmissions numbering in the hundreds.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 based on Monte Carlo simulation results.

claim: Median number of cross-species introductions observed in matching simulations is 592 (95% percentiles 311–811).
source: Median number of cross-species introductions observed in matching simulations is 592 (95% percentiles 311–811).
evidence: This is derived from Monte Carlo simulations matching empirical data.

claim: Recombination has been shown to occur in all genera of coronaviruses, including MERS-CoV.
source: Recombination has been shown to occur in all genera of coronaviruses, including MERS-CoV (Lai et al., 1985; Makino et al., 1986; Keck et al., 1988; Kottier et al., 1995; Herrewegh et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on coronavirus recombination.

claim: PHI and 3Seq methods consistently identify most of the apparent 'backbone' of the MERS-CoV phylogeny as encompassing sequences with evidence of recombination.
source: PHI and 3Seq methods consistently identify most of the apparent 'backbone' of the MERS-CoV phylogeny as encompassing sequences with evidence of recombination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on recombination detection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strong similarity in the grouping of human cases into outbreak clusters was found between genomic fragments.
source: We find strong similarity in the grouping of human cases into outbreak clusters between fragments (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A comparing phylogenies from different genome fragments.

claim: Human clusters are largely well-supported as monophyletic and consistent across trees of both genomic fragments.
source: Human clusters are largely well-supported as monophyletic and consistent across trees of both genomic fragments.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing marginal posterior probabilities.

claim: The same source-sink dynamics between camel and human populations were observed in trees constructed from separate genomic fragments as in the original full genome tree.
source: Additionally, we observe the same source-sink dynamics between camel and human populations in trees constructed from separate genomic fragments as were observed in the original full genome tree (Figures 1 and 4B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: There are 830,000 camels in Saudi Arabia.
source: We find there are 830,000 camels in Saudi Arabia (Abdallah and Faye, 2013) and that female camels in Saudi Arabia have an average fecundity of 45% (Abdallah and Faye, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature on camel populations.

claim: Female camels in Saudi Arabia have an average fecundity of 45%.
source: We find there are 830,000 camels in Saudi Arabia (Abdallah and Faye, 2013) and that female camels in Saudi Arabia have an average fecundity of 45% (Abdallah and Faye, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature on camel reproduction.

claim: The ratio of expected to empirical Neτ for MERS-CoV is less than the equivalent ratio for human measles virus.
source: This is less than the equivalent ratio for human measles virus (Bedford et al., 2011) and is in line with the expectation from neutral evolutionary dynamics plus some degree of transmission heterogeneity (Volz et al., 2013) and seasonal troughs in prevalence.
evidence: This is based on comparison to published measles virus analysis.

claim: The ladder-like appearance of the MERS-CoV tree can likely be explained by entirely demographic factors.
source: Thus, we believe that the ladder-like appearance of the MERS-CoV tree can likely be explained by entirely demographic factors.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of expected and empirical effective population sizes.

claim: Structured coalescent models can identify distinct demographic modes in MERS-CoV genomic data.
source: We showed that currently existing models of population structure (Vaughan et al., 2014) can identify distinct demographic modes in MERS-CoV genomic data, where viruses continuously circulating in camels repeatedly jump into humans and cause small outbreaks doomed to extinction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the structured coalescent analysis presented.

claim: Viruses continuously circulating in camels repeatedly jump into humans and cause small outbreaks doomed to extinction.
source: We showed that currently existing models of population structure (Vaughan et al., 2014) can identify distinct demographic modes in MERS-CoV genomic data, where viruses continuously circulating in camels repeatedly jump into humans and cause small outbreaks doomed to extinction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: At least 50 zoonotic introductions of MERS-CoV into humans from the reservoir were identified from sequence data.
source: From sequence data, we identify at least 50 zoonotic introductions of MERS-CoV into humans from the reservoir (Figure 1), from which we extrapolate that hundreds more such introductions must have taken place (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on structured coalescent analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hundreds more zoonotic introductions must have taken place beyond those identified from sequence data.
source: From sequence data, we identify at least 50 zoonotic introductions of MERS-CoV into humans from the reservoir (Figure 1), from which we extrapolate that hundreds more such introductions must have taken place (Figure 3).
evidence: This is extrapolated from Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: SARS-CoV caused a serious epidemic in humans in 2003, with over 8000 cases and nearly 800 deaths.
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) coronavirus, a Betacoronavirus like MERS-CoV, caused a serious epidemic in humans in 2003, with over 8000 cases and nearly 800 deaths.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SARS epidemic.

claim: SARS-CoV is a Betacoronavirus like MERS-CoV.
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) coronavirus, a Betacoronavirus like MERS-CoV, caused a serious epidemic in humans in 2003, with over 8000 cases and nearly 800 deaths.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge about coronaviruses.

claim: MERS-CoV's current R0 of ~0.7 is less than 1, but its proximity to the supercritical threshold raises alarm.
source: This leaves MERS-CoV in a precarious position; on one hand its current R0 of ∼0.7 is certainly less than 1, but its proximity to the supercritical threshold raises alarm.
evidence: This is based on the R0 estimates from Monte Carlo simulations and epidemiological interpretation.

claim: The final dataset consisted of 174 genomes from human infections and 100 genomes from camel infections.
source: The final dataset consisted of 174 genomes from human infections and 100 genomes from camel infections (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: Discrete trait analysis reconstruction identifies both camels and humans as important hosts for MERS-CoV persistence, but with humans as the ultimate source of camel infections.
source: Discrete trait analysis reconstruction identifies both camels and humans as important hosts for MERS-CoV persistence, but with humans as the ultimate source of camel infections.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 using discrete trait analysis.

claim: The discrete trait analysis interpretation of MERS-CoV evolution disagrees with lack of continuing human transmission chains outside of Arabian peninsula, low seroprevalence in humans and very high seroprevalence in camels across Saudi Arabia.
source: A similar approach has been attempted previously (Zhang et al., 2016), but this interpretation of MERS-CoV evolution disagrees with lack of continuing human transmission chains outside of Arabian peninsula, low seroprevalence in humans and very high seroprevalence in camels across Saudi Arabia.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing discrete trait results to epidemiological evidence.

claim: The discrete trait analysis reconstruction is likely false due to biased data and the inability of the model to account for vastly different rates of coalescence.
source: We suspect that this particular discrete trait analysis reconstruction is false due to biased data, that is, having nearly twice as many MERS-CoV sequences from humans (n=174) than from camels (n=100) and the inability of the model to account for and quantify vastly different rates of coalescence in the phylogenetic vicinity of both types of sequences.
evidence: This is an inference about model limitations based on data characteristics.

claim: The dataset has nearly twice as many MERS-CoV sequences from humans (n=174) than from camels (n=100).
source: We suspect that this particular discrete trait analysis reconstruction is false due to biased data, that is, having nearly twice as many MERS-CoV sequences from humans (n=174) than from camels (n=100) and the inability of the model to account for and quantify vastly different rates of coalescence in the phylogenetic vicinity of both types of sequences.
evidence: This describes the composition of the sequence dataset.

claim: Instances of human infection with MERS-CoV are more common than currently thought.
source: Our findings suggest that instances of human infection with MERS-CoV are more common than currently thought, with exceedingly short transmission chains mostly limited to primary cases that might be mild and ultimately not detected by surveillance or sequencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the large number of estimated introductions compared to observed cases.

claim: MERS-CoV transmission chains in humans are exceedingly short and mostly limited to primary cases that might be mild and ultimately not detected by surveillance or sequencing.
source: Our findings suggest that instances of human infection with MERS-CoV are more common than currently thought, with exceedingly short transmission chains mostly limited to primary cases that might be mild and ultimately not detected by surveillance or sequencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the low R0 and large number of estimated introductions.

claim: The combination of frequent spillover of MERS-CoV into humans and occasional outbreak amplification via poor hygiene practices appear sufficient to explain observed epidemiological patterns of MERS-CoV.
source: Given these findings, and the fact that large outbreaks of MERS occurred in hospitals, the combination of frequent spillover of MERS-CoV into humans and occasional outbreak amplification via poor hygiene practices (Assiri et al., 2013b; Chen et al., 2017) appear sufficient to explain observed epidemiological patterns of MERS-CoV.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis results and cited hospital outbreak studies.

claim: Large outbreaks of MERS occurred in hospitals.
source: Given these findings, and the fact that large outbreaks of MERS occurred in hospitals, the combination of frequent spillover of MERS-CoV into humans and occasional outbreak amplification via poor hygiene practices (Assiri et al., 2013b; Chen et al., 2017) appear sufficient to explain observed epidemiological patterns of MERS-CoV.
evidence: This is established from epidemiological reports cited.

claim: Contact with camels is a major risk factor for developing MERS, per WHO guidelines.
source: It is widely accepted that recorded human MERS-CoV infections are a result of at least several introductions of the virus into humans (Cotten et al., 2013) and that contact with camels is a major risk factor for developing MERS, per WHO guidelines (World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from WHO guidelines.

claim: Recorded human MERS-CoV infections are a result of at least several introductions of the virus into humans.
source: It is widely accepted that recorded human MERS-CoV infections are a result of at least several introductions of the virus into humans (Cotten et al., 2013) and that contact with camels is a major risk factor for developing MERS, per WHO guidelines (World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: As of 10 May 2017, the World Health Organization has been notified of 1952 cases of MERS-CoV.
source: As of 10 May 2017, the World Health Organization has been notified of 1952 cases of MERS-CoV (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from WHO data.

claim: Dispersion parameter ω was fixed to 0.1 following expectations from previous studies of coronavirus behavior.
source: 10,000 simulations were run for 121 uniformly spaced values of R0 across the range [0.5–1.1] with dispersion parameter ω fixed to 0.1 following expectations from previous studies of coronavirus behavior (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on cited previous studies of coronavirus transmission heterogeneity.

claim: The first sequences of MERS-CoV from camels do not appear in the data until November 2013.
source: The first sequences of MERS-CoV from camels do not appear in our data until November 2013.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the available sequence data.

claim: The finding of negligible human-to-camel transmission is robust to choice of prior.
source: Our finding of negligible human-to-camel transmission is robust to choice of prior (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing results under different priors.

claim: Human viruses appear as clusters of highly related sequences nested within the diversity seen in camel viruses.
source: This inference derives from the tree structure wherein human viruses appear as clusters of highly related sequences nested within the diversity seen in camel viruses, which themselves show significantly higher diversity and less clustering.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic pattern observed in Figure 1.

claim: Camel viruses show significantly higher diversity and less clustering than human viruses.
source: This inference derives from the tree structure wherein human viruses appear as clusters of highly related sequences nested within the diversity seen in camel viruses, which themselves show significantly higher diversity and less clustering.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic pattern observed in Figure 1.

claim: Dense terminal clusters of MERS-CoV circulating in humans are of no subsequent relevance to the evolution of the virus.
source: We observe dense terminal clusters of MERS-CoV circulating in humans that are of no subsequent relevance to the evolution of the virus.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic structure showing human clusters as terminal branches.

claim: Clusters of presumed human-to-human transmission are embedded within extensive diversity of MERS-CoV lineages inferred to be circulating in camels, a classic pattern of source-sink dynamics.
source: These clusters of presumed human-to-human transmission are then embedded within extensive diversity of MERS-CoV lineages inferred to be circulating in camels, a classic pattern of source-sink dynamics.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic pattern and interprets it using ecological theory.

claim: Structured coalescent analyses recover the camel-centered picture of MERS-CoV evolution despite sequence data heavily skewed towards non-uniformly sampled human cases.
source: Structured coalescent analyses recover the camel-centered picture of MERS-CoV evolution despite sequence data heavily skewed towards non-uniformly sampled human cases and are robust to choice of prior.
evidence: This summarizes the robustness of the structured coalescent results.
